To investigate the spawning ecology of Bridgelip sucker (Catostomus columbianus), researchers focused on the characteristics of the eggs and early developmental stages. It was determined that a newly emerged, water-hardened egg has a diameter typically ranging from 2.1 to 3 mm, which translates to a very modest initial wet weight of just 0.0082 grams [Wwb = 0.0082 grams], a value comparable to other small-bodied catostomids. This slight mass is consistent with a lecithotrophic larva absorbing its yolk reserves before transitioning to active feeding. The study was conducted entirely under controlled laboratory conditions, with the water temperature maintained at a stable 14 °C [T = 14 °C] throughout the incubation and larval rearing phases. This thermal regime is representative of the cool, spring-fed tributaries where this species typically spawns. The incubation period at this temperature extended for a specific duration, after which the sac-fry emerged and remained in the gravel interstices, continuing their dependence on the yolk sac.

As the Bridgelip sucker develops and progresses through its life stages, its body size increases dramatically from the initial hatchling mass. Growth is allometric, with the body plan reorganizing during the larval-juvenile transition. The species eventually attains a substantial ultimate total length of 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters], though available catch data from FishBase suggests a more typical total length of around 30 cm. Reaching these larger sizes requires considerable somatic investment. Based on the established length-weight relationship, an individual achieving this maximum length would have an estimated ultimate wet weight of approximately 1,060 grams [Wwi = approximately 1,060 grams]. This represents the upper end of the size spectrum for the species in most of its range, with larger individuals often being females who presumably benefit from the increased fecundity that a larger body cavity provides.

Sexual maturation in Catostomus columbianus is closely tied to the attainment of a specific body size rather than age alone, a common pattern in many freshwater teleosts. The onset of puberty and gonadal recrudescence is triggered once a fish reaches a total length of approximately 35.5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 35.5 centimeters], a value derived from measurements of fork length averaging 33.4 cm. At this developmental threshold, the estimated wet weight at puberty is roughly 516 grams [Wwp = roughly 516 grams], reflecting a significant investment in somatic growth before resources are directed toward reproductive effort. This size-based maturation strategy ensures that only individuals with sufficient energy reserves and body condition are able to initiate gametogenesis. The implication is that fish growing in less productive habitats or facing higher metabolic costs may reach this critical size later, thereby delaying their first spawning event.

At the stable water temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C] that characterizes their preferred spawning habitat, the annual reproductive output of a mature female Bridgelip sucker has been quantified. A female at the upper end of the size range produces an average of approximately 20,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 20,000 eggs per spawning event] and typically spawns once per year [F_R_i = spawns once per year] at this temperature. This substantial fecundity per event underscores the species' strategy of producing a large number of small, adhesive demersal eggs. These eggs are broadcast over suitable gravel substrates where they become lodged in the interstitial spaces, providing a measure of protection from predation and current.

Longevity data for Bridgelip sucker collected under these stable thermal conditions indicates a maximum lifespan of approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years], recorded in individuals maintained at a constant water temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. This relatively long lifespan is characteristic of a slow-growing, iteroparous fish that invests in multiple spawning events over its lifetime. The ability to survive for this extended period allows individuals to compensate for years of low reproductive success. This life-history strategy is common among catostomids adapted to cool, unproductive rivers, where energy surpluses are modest and the risk of reproductive failure is high. Consequently, the population dynamics of C. columbianus are likely driven more by adult survival than by exceptional recruitment in any single year. Such a strategy buffers the population against environmental stochasticity.
